# Cūḷamālukya Sutta (MN 63 (PTS MN i 426))

**ID:** MN 63 (PTS MN i 426)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Cūḷamālukya Sutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Shorter Discourse With Māluṅkya
**PTS:** MN i 426
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/mn63
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0202m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Cūḷamālukya Sutta* (MN 63; PTS MN i 426–432), also titled *Cūḷamālukyovāda Sutta*, is the sixty-third discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya* [Catalog; Davis and Flanagan 2014; Le 2018]. In this discourse, the monk Mālunkyāputta (or Mālunkāputta) approaches the Buddha demanding a definitive declaration on ten speculative metaphysical questions—whether the world is eternal or not eternal, finite or infinite, whether the soul and body are identical or different, and whether a Tathāgata exists, does not exist, both exists and does not exist, or neither exists nor does not exist after death—threatening to abandon the monastic life if these remain unexplained [SuttaCentral; Davis and Flanagan 2014; Galasek 2016]. The Buddha responds by pointing out that he never promised to explain these speculative matters, illustrating Mālunkyāputta's folly through the celebrated parable of a man pierced with a poisoned arrow who refuses the surgeon's help until he discovers the identity, caste, and physical characteristics of the archer, as well as the materials of the bow and arrow; such a man would die before obtaining answers to his irrelevant inquiries [Moult 2012; Davis and Flanagan 2014; Crosby 2014]. The Buddha states that these points are left undeclared (*avyākata*) because they are not beneficial, fundamental to the holy life, or conducive to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, calming, direct knowledge, and awakening [Foo Meng Jee 2013; Galasek 2016]. Scholars highlight the Buddha's pedagogical method of counter-questioning (*paṭipucchā*) deployed in the sutta to redirect the interlocutor toward liberation from suffering [Le 2018].

Curated parallels recorded on SuttaCentral include a discourse in the Chinese *Madhyama Āgama* (MĀ 221), an individual translation in the Taishō canon (T 94), and a citation in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitopadeśa* (T 1509.15) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus confirms alignment with the *Madhyama Āgama* (T 26, item 60) and identifies further text-reuse alignments across Tibetan translations—including Candrakīrti's *Prasannapadā* (D3860), the *Vinayakṣudravastu* (D0006-2), Śamathadeva's *Abhidharmakośaṭīkopayikā* (D4094-2), and Bhāviveka's *Prajñāpradīpaṭīkā* (D3859-3)—as well as Sanskrit texts like the *Dharmasaṃgraha* and Chinese Āgama collections (T 99 and T 1) [DharmaNexus]. Internally within the Pali canon, the discourse shares extensive segments on the undeclared views with the *Abyākata Saṁyutta* (SN 44), the *Vacchagotta Saṁyutta* (SN 33), and the *Poṭṭhapāda Sutta* (DN 9), as well as parts of the *Sacca Saṁyutta* (SN 56) and the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* [DharmaNexus; Galasek 2016]. English translations of the discourse have been made by I.B. Horner, Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli and Bhikkhu Bodhi, Thanissaro Bhikkhu, and Bhikkhu Sujato [SuttaCentral; Batchelor 1997; Hongladarom 2015].
